summary: Asks for comments on the instructions given to RFC authors, setting out how authors should prepare documents for the series. It was replaced by RFC 1543 and RFC 2223.

plainLanguage.summary: If you want to write one of these rule books, there is a how-to for it. This is a draft of the how-to, and people were asked what they think.

subtitle: Instructions for writing RFCs in consistent formats.

tldr.problem: RFC authors need clear, consistent formatting rules to ensure documents can be distributed and displayed correctly on many different systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1111 specifies format rules for two formats: ASCII with strict line and page limits, and PostScript with defined fonts, margins and sizing rules. Each RFC must include specific sections: a Status of this Memo section explaining the RFC's purpose, a distribution statement, and the author's address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1111 was replaced by RFC 1543 and RFC 2223, which updated the author guidelines as publication methods evolved.

today: RFC 1111 is Informational and historic. It has been superseded by RFC 1543 and RFC 2223, which provide updated instructions for RFC authors as distribution and publication methods evolved.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFCs are distributed as online files that people download and print or display on their own equipment. This means RFC format must work with a wide variety of printers and screens, from old ASCII terminals to modern graphical displays. The RFC Editor established strict formatting rules to ensure every RFC can be read reliably, no matter what equipment is used to view it.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet rule books are shared as files that people print out at home. The format has to work on any printer, so there are strict rules.

sections.title: Format Rules
sections.content: The RFC specifies two allowed formats: ASCII and PostScript. ASCII RFCs must use only ASCII character codes, with each page limited to 58 lines followed by a form feed, and each line limited to 72 characters. No overstriking or underlining is allowed. Text must be single-spaced within paragraphs with one blank line between paragraphs. Hyphenation at the right margin and footnotes are forbidden. PostScript RFCs use standard 8.5 by 11 inch pages with 1-inch margins on all sides, main text at minimum 10 points with 12-point line spacing, and only three fonts are acceptable: Helvetica, Times Roman and Courier. The RFC Editor may reformat submissions to match recent RFC styles, so authors should examine recent RFCs before submitting.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to write: plain text with very strict width and height rules, or fancy formatted documents with specific fonts and margins. Either way, it has to look the same on old and new equipment.

sections.title: Status and Distribution
sections.content: Each RFC must include a Status of this Memo section on the first page describing the RFC's purpose and how it should be understood. The RFC Editor and Internet Activities Board grant different statuses: Proposed Protocol for new protocol suggestions, Specification for standards meant for adoption, Discussion for exploring problems and solutions, Information for soliciting feedback, and Status for reporting on progress in Internet projects. A distribution statement is also required, typically stating that distribution is unlimited, though rare cases may restrict distribution in some way.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule book has to say at the top why it exists, and whether anyone can copy it or if there are limits.

sections.title: Required Sections and Relationships
sections.content: Every RFC must end with an Author's Address section. When an RFC relates to earlier RFCs, it uses two terms. OBSOLETES: this document completely replaces an earlier one with all the same information plus new information. UPDATES: this document adds to an earlier one and requires reading both. RFC indexes use OBSOLETED-BY and UPDATED-BY to point to newer documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Every rule book says who wrote it. If it replaces an older book, you can throw away the old one. If it just adds to it, you need to read both.

sections.title: Submission and Availability
sections.content: Authors must submit an editable online document to the RFC Editor, who may request minor format or style changes before assigning the RFC number. RFCs are announced to the SRI Network Information Center distribution list. The public can obtain RFCs via FTP from NIC.DDN.MIL using anonymous login, by email request to SERVICE@NIC.DDN.MIL, or through other information centers including the CSNET Information Center and NSFNET Information Service. As of the RFC's publication, Jon Postel was the RFC Editor.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors send their draft to the RFC Editor, who checks the format and assigns a number. Then people can download the finished rule book from several internet sites.
